lines.text: An island and a strip of mainland forest, once a Spanish colony, then a land of terror and of oil. This is the story of Equatorial Guinea.
In 1827 the British founded Port Clarence on the island of Bioko. Today it is Malabo, the capital.
Francisco Macias Nguema would become the first president, and his rule of terror drove a third of the people abroad.
Under Spain the colony of Spanish Guinea took shape, with cocoa plantations across Bioko.
Teodoro Obiang, Macias's own nephew, would overthrow him in 1979 and rule for decades after.
In 1968 Equatorial Guinea won independence from Spain, joining Bioko and the mainland of Rio Muni.
Eric Moussambani won hearts at the 2000 Olympics, a swimmer who struggled bravely through his race.
By now oil had been found offshore. In 2004 a band of foreign mercenaries plotted a coup, and failed.
In 2012 the country hosted the Africa Cup of Nations together with Gabon.
And in the mainland forest, a new capital is rising, Ciudad de la Paz, the City of Peace.
Rich in oil yet ruled by one family, Equatorial Guinea's story is still being written.
